summary: Defines the flexible file layout type for Parallel NFS. Metadata lives on one server while file data is stored on separate storage devices, and those devices need only limited interaction with the metadata server and can use existing protocols. It also supports client-side mirroring.

eli5.summary: A librarian keeps the catalog while the books sit in many rooms. Readers ask the librarian where a book is, then go straight to that room.

questions: how does parallel nfs separate metadata from data
what is the pnfs flexible file layout
what is client side mirroring in pnfs
difference between loose and tight coupling in pnfs
subtitle: A pNFS layout that sends clients straight to ordinary NFS servers for file data, with mirroring done by the client.

tldr.problem: Parallel NFS separates metadata from data, but storage systems differ, and many data servers speak plain NFSv3 or NFSv4 and cannot take part in a rich control protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The flexible file layout tells the client which NFS storage devices hold each stripe and mirror, plus credentials to use. Loosely coupled devices are controlled with synthetic user and group ids, and the client updates every mirror.
tldr.outcome: A metadata server can use existing NFS servers as data servers, fence clients by changing ids, and repair mirrors from client error reports. Loose coupling cannot protect against malicious clients.

today: RFC 8435 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2018. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Definitions
sections.content:
In Parallel NFS (pNFS), the metadata server (MDS) returns layout structures that say where file data lives. Different layout types suit different storage systems. This RFC defines the flexible file layout type, used with file-based data servers that are accessed with NFSv3 (RFC 1813), NFSv4.0 (RFC 7530), NFSv4.1 (RFC 5661) and NFSv4.2 (RFC 7862).

The control protocol described here is based on NFS and does not pass stateids between the metadata server and the storage devices. Instead the storage devices are set up so the metadata server has full access rights to the data file system, and it uses synthetic ids to control client access to individual files. The RFC also adds client-side mirroring, where the client, not the server, updates every copy of a file segment.
sections.eli5: The catalog librarian knows where everything is, but the books are in other rooms, and the readers fetch them directly.

sections.title: Loose and Tight Coupling, Fencing and Locking
sections.content:
A server may choose a loosely coupled or tightly coupled model between the metadata server and the storage devices. NFSv3 and NFSv4.0 devices are always treated as loosely coupled. NFSv4.1+ devices that do not set EXCHGID4_FLAG_USE_PNFS_DS in EXCHANGE_ID are loosely coupled too, and those that do can potentially be tightly coupled through a back-end control protocol that this RFC does not define.

In the loose model, fencing works by changing the synthetic uid and gid that own the data file on the storage device. The layout hands the client the user and group to put in its RPC credentials (ffds_user and ffds_group). When the owner changes, old credentials fail with NFS4ERR_ACCESS. The metadata server cannot fence a single client, so it fences all clients, and they then fetch new layouts. Synthetic ids of 0 SHOULD be avoided under AUTH_SYS. In the tight model, the data file gets the same owner, mode bits and ACL as the metadata file, and fencing is left to the control protocol, with NFS4ERR_BAD_STATEID as the client-visible error.

For locking, loosely coupled I/O uses the anonymous stateid, so mandatory byte-range locking cannot be supported, and share reservations are enforced by the client. Tightly coupled devices can support mandatory locks when both sides support them.

Regardless of model, if any WRITE to a storage device did not use stable_how equal to FILE_SYNC, a LAYOUTCOMMIT to the metadata server MUST be preceded by a COMMIT to the storage devices.
sections.eli5: If the librarian wants to lock you out of a room, she changes the lock code. In the loose model she has to change it for everybody, and then she gives the new code to the people who are allowed in.

sections.title: Device Addressing and Multipathing
sections.content:
Clients learn a storage device's network address with the NFSv4.1+ GETDEVICEINFO operation. It returns an ff_device_addr4 holding ffda_netaddrs, a list of one or more addresses, and ffda_versions, an array of choices of NFS version, minor version and coupling strength. This layout defines semantics for ffdv_version 3 and 4. If it is 3, the server MUST set the minor version to 0 and ffdv_tightly_coupled to false, and the client MUST use NFSv3.

ffdv_rsize and ffdv_wsize carry the maximum read and write sizes the device supports. If ffdv_tightly_coupled is not set, the client MUST commit its writes to stable storage before sending LAYOUTCOMMIT.

Listing several addresses gives multipathing, which supports bandwidth scaling by trunking and higher availability. The client may switch to another address without asking for a new layout. If no address responds, the client SHOULD send GETDEVICEINFO to replace the mappings. If a client cannot use any offered version combination, it reports NFS4ERR_MINOR_VERS_MISMATCH through LAYOUTRETURN or LAYOUTERROR, then either retries GETDEVICEINFO or sends I/O through the metadata server.
sections.eli5: Each room may have several doors. If one door is stuck, you try another, and you only go back to the librarian if none work.

sections.title: The Layout and Striping
sections.content:
The layout body is an ff_layout4. It contains ffl_stripe_unit (the stripe unit size), ffl_mirrors (an array of mirrors, each an ff_mirror4 listing data servers), ffl_flags and ffl_stats_collect_hint, a hint in seconds for how often the client should report LAYOUTSTATS. A file may be built from more than one layout segment, and each segment MAY use different striping. The number of stripes is the number of data servers within each mirror, and if there is only one stripe, the stripe unit MUST be zero. Stripe unit and stripe count are assumed the same across all mirrors.

Each ff_data_server4 carries a device id, an efficiency value (higher means higher perceived utility), a stateid, an array of filehandles (ffds_fh_vers, exactly one per entry in ffda_versions) and the synthetic user and group. For loose coupling the stateid MUST be the anonymous stateid. For tight coupling, the client MUST ignore the user and group.

Only a sparse mapping is supported: the logical offset in the file is also the physical offset on the storage device, which leaves holes on devices that do not hold a given stripe. With stripe width W as the number of data servers, the bytes in a stripe are S = W * ffl_stripe_unit, and the stripe number is N = L / S for logical offset L.
sections.eli5: The map says how the pages of a big book are dealt out to the rooms, and each page keeps the same page number in its room, so the other rooms have gaps.

sections.title: Mirroring and Error Recovery
sections.content:
With client-side mirroring, the metadata server decides how many copies exist and where, and the client cannot dictate devices. The client decides which mirror to read from, because it knows its own network paths better than the metadata server. ffds_efficiency should not reflect network distance for that reason.

For writes, unless FF_FLAGS_WRITE_ONE_MIRROR is set, the client must update every mirror it is given, and one failed update fails the whole operation. If the flag is set, the client updates one mirror and the storage device MUST update the rest. Errors are reported to the metadata server with LAYOUTRETURN or LAYOUTERROR. After an error, the client MUST NOT assume the next layout matches the previous one, and MUST resend any updates not committed to all mirrors. Once a COMMIT is answered, all replicas must reflect the writes on stable storage.

The metadata server can resilver (rebuild) a mirror at any time, and MUST recall the writable layout segments it is resilvering. During that time it can answer LAYOUTGET with NFS4ERR_LAYOUTUNAVAILABLE, and the client does its I/O through the metadata server. For I/O errors in general, the client MUST report them with ff_ioerr4 at LAYOUTRETURN, the metadata server MUST recall outstanding layouts for the affected stripes, and it MUST finish recovery before issuing new ones.
sections.eli5: If you make a photocopy, you must put one in every room that keeps a copy. If one room is closed, tell the librarian, who will fix it.

sections.title: Flags, Reports and Recalls
sections.content:
The ffl_flags bitmap lets the metadata server describe conditions that follow from tighter or looser coupling. FF_FLAGS_NO_IO_THRU_MDS is only a hint, and the client can still send I/O to the metadata server.

On LAYOUTRETURN, the client uses ff_layoutreturn4 to report I/O errors (ff_ioerr4) and, optionally, usage statistics (ff_iostats4) for hot byte ranges. With NFSv4.2, it MAY use LAYOUTERROR and LAYOUTSTATS instead of waiting. Statistics are cumulative, and times are stored as durations rather than dates. A client may also pass a hint with the number of mirrors it wants (ff_layouthint4), which the server can ignore.

The metadata server should recall layouts when security policy changes, when the layout changes, when locking constraints conflict, and for resilvering. CB_RECALL_ANY with mask bits 16 (read) and 17 (read/write) lets it ask for layouts back to reclaim resources. If a client's lease expires or it fails to return a recalled layout, the server MAY revoke its layouts, and MUST fence it from the data files.
sections.eli5: Readers can leave notes about problems or how busy a room was. The librarian can also ask for books back when things change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The metadata server enforces access control at LAYOUTGET time and, if access is allowed, hands the client the credentials for the requested iomode. The client sees filehandles of file objects only, not directories, so it cannot guess a parent directory's filehandle, and knowing one file's synthetic ids does not necessarily give access to another data file.

When a file's permissions or ACL change, the metadata server SHOULD recall all layouts and MUST fence any client still holding one before committing to the new permissions. With loose coupling, access control works against cooperative clients but cannot stop malicious ones, so it is equivalent to AUTH_SYS, and the link between metadata server and storage device SHOULD be secure from eavesdropping and tampering. This layout type does not support RPCSEC_GSS with the loosely coupled model. With tight coupling the storage device can validate credentials through the control protocol, so RPCSEC_GSS raises no extra issues there.
sections.eli5: The key code only opens one room, so knowing it does not help you get into others. But the system trusts readers to be honest, so it is not a bank vault.

items.label: FF_FLAGS_NO_LAYOUTCOMMIT
items.desc: Client is not required to send LAYOUTCOMMIT to the metadata server.

items.label: FF_FLAGS_NO_IO_THRU_MDS
items.desc: Client should not send I/O to the metadata server; a hint only.

items.label: FF_FLAGS_NO_READ_IO
items.desc: Client should not send READs with a read/write layout; ask for a read layout instead.

items.label: FF_FLAGS_WRITE_ONE_MIRROR
items.desc: Client needs to update only one mirror.
